questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Staff on an inpatient behavioral health unit report that a 30-year-old client drank about 8 L of tap water during the day. The evening serum sodium is 126 mEq/L, down from 139 mEq/L this morning. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Offer salty snacks to bring the sodium level back up
Notify the provider of the sodium result and the reported water intake
Encourage more fluids so the kidneys can flush out the extra water
Recheck the sodium level with the routine labs tomorrow morning
optionRationales: Incorrect. The problem is excess water diluting the sodium, not too little salt; snacks do not address the cause, and the provider needs to know about the rapid drop.
Correct. A sodium of 126 is hyponatremia caused by dilution; the rapid drop needs prompt provider notification along with the likely cause.
Incorrect. More water lowers the concentration of sodium even further.
Incorrect. A large, rapid change in sodium should not wait for routine labs.
questions.rationale: A serum sodium is a concentration, like the strength of lemonade: add a lot of water and it gets weaker even though the amount of sodium has not changed. Drinking about 8 L of water in a day diluted this client's sodium from 139 to 126 mEq/L, which is hyponatremia (below 135). Because sodium is the water regulator and a rapid fall is a significant change, the nurse notifies the provider promptly with the result and the cause. Offering salty snacks is tempting because it seems to "replace sodium," but the problem is too much water, not too little salt.
questions.takeaway: A falling sodium after large water intake is dilution; report it and stop adding water.
questions.hintContent: Think of sodium as a concentration that depends on how much water is in the body.
questions.hintStrategy: For a rapid lab change with a clear cause, the first action is to report both; eliminate options that add more of the cause.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 59-year-old client has been receiving IV magnesium replacement for hypomagnesemia. This morning's magnesium is 2.9 mEq/L, and another dose is scheduled now. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the dose as scheduled, since magnesium was low yesterday
Give half of the dose and recheck the level this evening
Hold the dose and notify the provider of the new result
Give the dose and ask dietary to add magnesium-rich foods
optionRationales: Incorrect. The prescription was based on yesterday's low value; today's result shows the problem has reversed.
Incorrect. The nurse cannot change the dose without a prescription, and any added magnesium is inappropriate now.
Correct. A magnesium of 2.9 mEq/L is above the normal 1.5–2.5 range (hypermagnesemia); giving more would raise it further, so the nurse holds and reports.
Incorrect. Adding magnesium from both medication and food would worsen the high level.
questions.rationale: The normal magnesium range is 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, so 2.9 is hypermagnesemia. Before giving any electrolyte replacement, the nurse checks the most recent level to evaluate whether the treatment has worked or overshot. Because more magnesium would raise an already high level, the nurse holds the dose and notifies the provider. Giving it as scheduled is tempting because the order exists, but an order based on yesterday's data does not fit today's result.
questions.takeaway: Check the latest level before every electrolyte replacement; hold and report if it is now above normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal magnesium range and compare it with the new result.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, compare the newest data with the reason the order was written; if the reason is gone, hold and clarify.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 76-year-old client's serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L, and the nurse has notified the provider. While waiting for prescriptions, which assessment is the priority?
options: Skin turgor on the sternum
Urine specific gravity
Mucous membrane moisture
Heart rate and rhythm
optionRationales: Incorrect. Skin turgor reflects fluid volume, not the effect of a potassium imbalance, and is less reliable in older adults.
Incorrect. Specific gravity reflects urine concentration and does not show potassium's most dangerous effect.
Incorrect. Mucous membranes help assess fluid volume, not the risk created by a high potassium.
Correct. Potassium is the cardiac electrolyte that maintains normal heart rhythm, so the heart rate and rhythm are the priority assessment.
questions.rationale: Each electrolyte has a main job, and that job tells the nurse what to watch. Potassium regulates nerve impulse conduction, muscle contraction, and especially normal cardiac rhythm, which is why it is called the cardiac electrolyte. With hyperkalemia, the most important assessment is the heart rate and rhythm. The fluid-status assessments are tempting because they appear in every fluid and electrolyte exam, but they do not monitor the danger that potassium creates.
questions.takeaway: Potassium out of range: assess the heart first.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nickname for potassium and what it controls.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the abnormal lab to the body system it affects most, then choose the assessment of that system.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 28-year-old marathon runner drank about 6 L of plain water during and after a race and now has a serum sodium of 130 mEq/L. The runner says, "How can my sodium be low? I ate a salty meal last night." Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "The sodium level is a concentration, so a lot of water dilutes it."
"The salty meal was used up, so your body has no sodium left."
"Running destroys cells that normally store sodium inside them."
"Your kidneys stopped absorbing salt from food during the race."
optionRationales: Correct. A serum sodium reflects how much water the sodium is dissolved in; large amounts of plain water lower the concentration.
Incorrect. The body still has sodium; 130 mEq/L is low, not zero, and the problem is extra water.
Incorrect. Sodium is mainly an extracellular electrolyte; cell breakdown releases potassium and phosphate.
Incorrect. Sodium comes from the diet through the gut, and this explanation does not account for the large water intake.
questions.rationale: Sodium is the main ECF electrolyte and the body's water regulator, and its lab value is a concentration. It depends on both how much sodium is taken in and how much water is in the body. Drinking a large volume of plain water dilutes the sodium even after a salty meal, producing hyponatremia (below 135 mEq/L). The cell-breakdown option is tempting because it explains other lab changes, but cells release potassium and phosphate, not sodium.
questions.takeaway: Serum sodium is a concentration: more water lowers it, less water raises it.
questions.hintContent: Use the lemonade analogy: what happens to the strength when water is added?
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that uses the key data in the stem (6 L of plain water).

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 44-year-old client with metabolic acidosis asks the nurse, "Which foods should I eat to get more bicarbonate?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Leafy greens and bananas are the best sources of bicarbonate."
"Your body makes bicarbonate; your kidneys produce and reabsorb it as needed."
"Dairy products such as milk and cheese supply most bicarbonate."
"Table salt and canned soups are good sources of bicarbonate."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Leafy greens and bananas are potassium sources, not bicarbonate sources.
Correct. Bicarbonate is produced by the body and regulated by the kidneys, which generate and reabsorb it; it is not obtained from the diet.
Incorrect. Dairy foods are sources of calcium and phosphate.
Incorrect. Salt and canned soups are sources of sodium and chloride.
questions.rationale: Bicarbonate is unique among the major electrolytes: it is found in both the ECF and ICF, it acts as the body's main buffer, and it is made by the body rather than taken in from food. The kidneys generate bicarbonate and reabsorb it as needed to keep blood pH stable. The distractors each name real sources of other electrolytes, which makes them tempting for a student who knows food lists but forgets that bicarbonate is homemade.
questions.takeaway: Bicarbonate comes from the body (kidneys), not from food.
questions.hintContent: Which major electrolyte is the one the body produces itself?
questions.hintStrategy: When every distractor is a real food source, ask whether this electrolyte comes from food at all.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with heart failure asks, "Why does my ankle swelling get worse after I eat salty food?" Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Salt pulls water out of your blood vessels and into your cells."
"Salt makes your kidneys release extra water, so fluid pools in your legs."
"Water follows sodium, so extra salt makes your body hold on to more fluid."
"Salt breaks down the protein that keeps fluid inside your vessels."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sodium stays mainly outside the cells, so it holds water in the extracellular space rather than moving it into cells.
Incorrect. Extra sodium makes the body hold on to water, not release it.
Correct. Sodium is the water regulator of the ECF; where sodium goes, water follows, so a high sodium intake increases ECF volume.
Incorrect. Albumin keeps fluid in the vessels; salt does not break it down.
questions.rationale: Sodium is the main extracellular electrolyte and controls water balance, summed up as "water follows sodium." It also affects serum osmolality and ECF volume. When a client eats a lot of salt, the body holds on to more water in the extracellular space, which in heart failure shows up as edema and weight gain. The option about salt pulling water into cells is tempting because it mentions water movement, but sodium keeps water outside the cells.
questions.takeaway: Water follows sodium: more salt in, more fluid held in the ECF.
questions.hintContent: Recall the short phrase that describes sodium's main job.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the explanation built on the core principle of the electrolyte, not one that sounds technical.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 63-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease reports eating a usual diet and has no recent injury or illness. Today's phosphate is 6.0 mg/dL. Which explanation best accounts for this result?
options: Damaged cells are releasing their stored phosphate into the blood
The client is eating far more dairy and meat than usual
The sample was hemolyzed, which falsely lowered the phosphate
The failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate, so it builds up in the blood
optionRationales: Incorrect. Cell breakdown raises phosphate after trauma, chemotherapy, or extreme illness, none of which applies here.
Incorrect. The client reports a usual diet, so increased intake does not explain the result.
Incorrect. This result is high, not low, so a falsely lowered value does not fit.
Correct. The kidneys normally excrete phosphate; when they fail, phosphate accumulates, producing hyperphosphatemia.
questions.rationale: The normal phosphate range is 2.5–4.5 mg/dL, so 6.0 is hyperphosphatemia. When a value is high, the nurse asks what is adding the electrolyte or what is keeping the body from getting rid of it. In kidney failure, the kidneys can no longer excrete phosphate, so it builds up. Cell breakdown is the tempting answer because it also raises phosphate, but the stem rules out injury and illness.
questions.takeaway: Kidney failure raises phosphate because the kidneys cannot excrete it.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the high value comes from added intake, cell breakdown, or poor removal.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the details that rule causes out (usual diet, no injury) to eliminate options.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client receiving dialysis has been taught to limit high-phosphate foods. Which snack choice indicates that the client understood the teaching?
options: Fresh apple slices
Cheese and whole-grain crackers
A cup of yogurt
A handful of mixed nuts
optionRationales: Correct. Fresh fruit such as an apple is not one of the main phosphate sources (dairy, meat and fish, nuts, and whole grains).
Incorrect. Cheese (dairy) and whole grains are both phosphate sources.
Incorrect. Yogurt is a dairy product, a major phosphate source.
Incorrect. Nuts are a phosphate source.
questions.rationale: Phosphate is needed for ATP production, bone and teeth formation, and acid–base balance, and it comes from the diet. Its common sources are dairy products, meat and fish, nuts, and whole grains. Because failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate, clients on dialysis are often taught to limit these foods. Cheese and whole-grain crackers are tempting because they seem like a sensible snack, but they combine two phosphate sources.
questions.takeaway: Phosphate sources: dairy, meat and fish, nuts, and whole grains.
questions.hintContent: List the food groups that supply phosphate and see which option avoids all of them.
questions.hintStrategy: For "understood the teaching" items, eliminate every option that still contains the restricted item.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 62-year-old client who is lactose intolerant has a total calcium of 8.6 mg/dL. The client says, "I can't drink milk, so I guess I can't get calcium from food." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Bananas and potatoes are the best non-dairy sources of calcium for you."
"Leafy greens and calcium-fortified foods help, and vitamin D aids absorption."
"Without milk, the only way to get calcium is through a supplement."
"Your body makes its own calcium, so diet doesn't really matter."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Bananas and potatoes are potassium sources, not calcium sources.
Correct. Calcium sources include dairy, leafy green vegetables, and fortified foods, and vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium.
Incorrect. Non-dairy foods such as leafy greens and fortified foods also supply calcium.
Incorrect. Calcium must come from the diet; bicarbonate is the electrolyte the body makes.
questions.rationale: A total calcium of 8.6 mg/dL is below the course range of 9–11 mg/dL, so it is hypocalcemia. Calcium is needed for bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signals, and blood clotting, and it comes from dairy, leafy green vegetables, and fortified foods, with vitamin D helping absorption. A client who avoids dairy for cultural, digestive, or personal reasons can still meet needs with other sources. The supplement-only option is tempting, but it ignores food choices that fit the client.
questions.takeaway: Calcium sources beyond dairy: leafy greens and fortified foods, with vitamin D to help absorption.
questions.hintContent: Recall all the calcium sources, not just dairy, and the vitamin that helps absorption.
questions.hintStrategy: The best teaching response corrects the misconception and gives practical options that fit the client's situation.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 85-year-old client has eaten and drunk very little for 5 days because of a viral illness and has no vomiting or diarrhea. The potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. The client's daughter asks, "How can her potassium be low if she isn't losing anything?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: "Her body has used up the potassium it stores in her bones."
"Low intake makes the cells release potassium into the blood."
"Her kidneys keep getting rid of potassium even when she isn't taking any in."
"Not drinking water has concentrated her blood and lowered the potassium."
optionRationales: Incorrect. The body does not store potassium in bone; bone stores calcium and phosphate.
Incorrect. Cells release potassium when they are injured or die, which would raise, not lower, the serum level.
Correct. The body does not store potassium, and the kidneys continue to excrete it even when intake stops, so the level falls when the client does not eat.
Incorrect. Concentrated blood would tend to raise a concentration, not lower it.
questions.rationale: Potassium is the main intracellular electrolyte and the cardiac electrolyte. The body does not store it, so it must be consumed daily, and the kidneys keep excreting it even when intake stops. A client who eats very little for several days can therefore develop hypokalemia (below 3.5 mEq/L) without any GI losses. The option about bone stores is tempting because calcium is stored there, but potassium has no reserve.
questions.takeaway: No potassium intake means the level falls, because the body has no store and the kidneys keep excreting it.
questions.hintContent: Recall whether the body keeps a reserve of potassium and what the kidneys do when intake stops.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that would move the lab in the opposite direction from the result in the stem.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with a serum potassium of 5.7 mEq/L has a new prescription for a potassium-restricted diet. The nurse checks the lunch tray before it is served. Which items should the nurse remove? Select all that apply.
options: Sliced banana
Baked potato
Spinach salad
Black bean soup
White rice
Gelatin dessert
optionRationales: Correct. Bananas are a major potassium source.
Correct. Potatoes are a major potassium source.
Correct. Leafy greens such as spinach are a potassium source.
Correct. Beans are a potassium source.
Incorrect. White rice is not one of the main potassium sources and fits the restriction.
Incorrect. Gelatin is not a potassium source and fits the restriction.
questions.rationale: A potassium of 5.7 mEq/L is hyperkalemia (above 5.0). Common potassium sources are bananas, potatoes, leafy greens, beans, and avocados, so these are the items to remove for a client on a potassium restriction. The nurse checks the tray before the client eats rather than after. Spinach salad is easy to leave on the tray because it seems like a healthy choice, but leafy greens are a potassium source.
questions.takeaway: Potassium sources: bananas, potatoes, leafy greens, beans, and avocados.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five potassium sources and check each tray item against them.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each food as a true/false question: is it a potassium source?

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews a 50-year-old client's electrolyte panel (see exhibit). Which results should the nurse report as outside the normal range? Select all that apply.
options: Sodium 144 mEq/L
Potassium 5.3 mEq/L
Chloride 101 mEq/L
Magnesium 1.3 mEq/L
Phosphate 4.8 mg/dL
Total calcium 9.6 mg/dL
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sodium 144 is within 135–145 mEq/L.
Correct. Potassium 5.3 is above 5.0 mEq/L, hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Chloride 101 is within 95–105 mEq/L.
Correct. Magnesium 1.3 is below 1.5 mEq/L, hypomagnesemia.
Correct. Phosphate 4.8 is above 4.5 mg/dL, hyperphosphatemia.
Incorrect. Calcium 9.6 is within the 9–11 mg/dL range.
questions.rationale: The course ranges are sodium 135–145, potassium 3.5–5.0, chloride 95–105, and magnesium 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, with calcium 9–11 and phosphate 2.5–4.5 mg/dL. Values close to a limit are the easiest to misread: a potassium of 5.3 looks close to normal but is hyperkalemia, and sodium 144 looks high but is still normal. Comparing each result with its exact range, and noticing the units, prevents both missed and false alarms.
questions.takeaway: Compare each electrolyte to its exact range; values near the limit are the ones most often misread.
questions.hintContent: Recall each normal range and check whether the value falls inside it.
questions.hintStrategy: Go line by line and decide in or out for each value; do not let one abnormal result bias the others.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a caseload for clients at risk for elevated serum potassium and phosphate caused by cell breakdown. Which clients are at risk? Select all that apply.
options: A client who received chemotherapy for a large lymphoma yesterday
A client with extensive muscle damage after a crush injury
A client with severe sepsis and multiple organ failure
A client who drank 5 L of plain water in one afternoon
A client with a nasogastric tube to suction for 3 days
A client who is NPO and receiving plain D5W
optionRationales: Correct. Chemotherapy destroys tumor cells, which release intracellular potassium and phosphate.
Correct. Crushed muscle cells release their intracellular contents into the blood.
Correct. Extreme illness can cause widespread cell injury and death.
Incorrect. Excess water dilutes the blood, lowering sodium; it does not break cells open.
Incorrect. Gastric suction removes chloride-rich secretions; it does not cause cell breakdown.
Incorrect. An NPO client on plain D5W is at risk for low potassium from lack of intake.
questions.rationale: Potassium and phosphate live mainly inside cells. When cells are injured or die, as with chemotherapy, trauma, or extreme illness, their contents spill into the blood and serum levels rise without any change in intake. The other clients have real electrolyte risks, but in the opposite direction or involving other electrolytes. The NPO client is tempting because potassium is involved, but lack of intake lowers potassium.
questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy, trauma, and extreme illness can raise potassium and phosphate through cell breakdown.
questions.hintContent: Ask which situations break cells open and release their contents.
questions.hintStrategy: Check both the electrolyte and the direction of change for each client.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 61-year-old client with hypertension has been told to reduce sodium intake. The client asks which foods to limit. Which items should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Canned vegetable soup
Processed deli meats
Salt added at the table
Frozen packaged dinners
Fresh apples and pears
Plain cooked oatmeal
optionRationales: Correct. Canned foods and soups are common sodium sources.
Correct. Processed foods are high in sodium.
Correct. Table salt is sodium chloride.
Correct. Packaged and processed foods are a major source of sodium.
Incorrect. Fresh fruit is not a significant sodium source.
Incorrect. Plain oatmeal without added salt is not a significant sodium source.
questions.rationale: Sodium and chloride share their main dietary sources: table salt, processed foods, soups, and canned foods. Many clients think only of the salt shaker, but processed and canned foods often supply most of the day's sodium. Because water follows sodium, cutting these foods helps limit extra ECF volume. Canned soup is the item most often missed, since it does not taste as salty as chips.
questions.takeaway: Sodium hides in processed, canned, and packaged foods, not just the salt shaker.
questions.hintContent: Recall the common sources of sodium and chloride.
questions.hintStrategy: In diet SATA, check each food against the taught source list rather than how salty it tastes.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 54-year-old client with chronic alcohol use has a magnesium of 1.2 mEq/L and a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L that has not risen after 2 days of oral potassium chloride. The provider adds IV magnesium sulfate. Which statements by the nurse explaining this plan to a nursing student are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: "Magnesium activates the sodium–potassium pump that holds potassium in cells."
"While magnesium stays low, potassium keeps leaking away despite replacement."
"Correcting the magnesium also makes a low calcium easier to raise."
"Low magnesium can make the nerves and muscles less stable."
"Once the magnesium is given, the potassium replacement is no longer needed."
"Magnesium is mainly an extracellular electrolyte, like sodium."
optionRationales: Correct. Magnesium switches on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which moves potassium into cells; without it, potassium is hard to hold on to.
Correct. Low magnesium lets potassium keep leaking away, which is why this client's potassium has not risen with replacement alone.
Correct. The body needs magnesium to regulate calcium normally, so calcium is hard to raise until magnesium is corrected.
Correct. Magnesium is the stabilizer electrolyte that helps regulate neuromuscular activity.
Incorrect. Magnesium lets the potassium replacement work; it does not replace potassium, so the client still needs potassium.
Incorrect. Magnesium lives mainly inside the cells, like potassium and phosphate; sodium is the main extracellular electrolyte.
questions.rationale: Magnesium, the stabilizer electrolyte, lives mainly inside cells. It activates the sodium–potassium pump, regulates neuromuscular activity, and is needed for normal calcium regulation. When magnesium is low, potassium keeps leaking away and calcium stays hard to raise no matter how much is given, so magnesium is replaced first and the other replacements can then work. A magnesium of 1.2 mEq/L is hypomagnesemia (below 1.5), which explains why this client's potassium has not responded. The statement that potassium is no longer needed is tempting because magnesium "fixes" the potassium problem, but magnesium only lets the potassium replacement stay; it does not supply potassium.
questions.takeaway: Low potassium that will not correct? Check magnesium; replace it first so potassium (and calcium) replacement can work.
questions.hintContent: Recall magnesium's nickname and why it is replaced before potassium and calcium.
questions.hintStrategy: For each statement, ask whether it explains why magnesium comes first or confuses magnesium with another electrolyte.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 39-year-old client with metabolic acidosis is receiving lactated Ringer's and asks about bicarbonate. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: "Bicarbonate is found both inside and outside your cells."
"Your kidneys make bicarbonate and reabsorb it as needed."
"Bicarbonate buffers acid to keep your blood pH stable."
"The lactate in your IV is converted into bicarbonate."
"You can raise your bicarbonate by eating more leafy greens."
"Bicarbonate is a positively charged ion, like sodium."
optionRationales: Correct. Bicarbonate is the electrolyte found in both the ECF and ICF.
Correct. The kidneys generate bicarbonate and reabsorb it as needed.
Correct. Bicarbonate is the body's main buffer, regulating acid–base balance.
Correct. The liver converts the lactate in LR to bicarbonate, which helps correct metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate is made by the body, not obtained from food.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is an anion, carrying a negative charge.
questions.rationale: Bicarbonate is unique: it is found in both the ECF and ICF, it buffers acid to keep blood pH stable, and it is produced by the body, with the kidneys generating and reabsorbing it as needed. The lactate in lactated Ringer's is converted to bicarbonate, which is why LR helps correct metabolic acidosis. The leafy-greens option is tempting because diet is the source of most electrolytes, but bicarbonate is the exception.
questions.takeaway: Bicarbonate: found on both sides of the cell, made by the body, controlled by the kidneys, and boosted by LR's lactate.
questions.hintContent: Recall what makes bicarbonate "unique" compared with other electrolytes.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement for location, source, job, and charge.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · The Electrolytes: Roles, Sources & Lab Values
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is identifying clients who need close monitoring for a falling serum potassium. Which clients are at risk? Select all that apply.
options: A client NPO for 4 days receiving IV fluid with no added potassium
A client taking furosemide twice daily
A client with 3 days of repeated vomiting
A client 1 day after a severe crush injury to both legs
A client whose sample was reported as hemolyzed
A client who received chemotherapy for a large tumor yesterday
optionRationales: Correct. The body does not store potassium, and the kidneys keep excreting it, so no intake leads to a falling level.
Correct. Loop diuretics such as furosemide increase potassium loss in the urine.
Correct. Vomiting removes potassium-containing fluid while intake is usually poor.
Incorrect. Crushed cells release potassium, so the level tends to rise.
Incorrect. A hemolyzed sample falsely raises the potassium result.
Incorrect. Tumor cell breakdown after chemotherapy tends to raise potassium.
questions.rationale: Potassium must be taken in every day because the body does not store it, and the kidneys keep excreting it even when intake stops. Clients who are NPO without potassium replacement, who take potassium-wasting diuretics, or who are losing GI fluids are at risk for hypokalemia. Cell breakdown from trauma or chemotherapy, and hemolysis in the tube, push the result the other way. The crush-injury client is tempting because potassium is a concern, but the risk is a rising level.
questions.takeaway: No intake, diuretics, and GI losses lower potassium; cell breakdown and hemolysis raise it.
questions.hintContent: For each client, decide whether potassium is being lost or released.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort the options into "potassium falling" and "potassium rising" before selecting.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · Fluid & Electrolyte Assessment, Daily Weights & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 9-month-old is receiving IV fluids for dehydration from gastroenteritis. Four hours later, the infant is irritable and difficult to console, and the nurse finds that the anterior fontanel is bulging. What should the nurse do?
options: Document it as a sign that the infant is now rehydrated
Increase the IV rate to finish rehydration sooner
Offer oral fluids and reassess the fontanel in 4 hours
Report the bulging fontanel to the provider promptly
optionRationales: Incorrect. Successful rehydration returns the fontanel to soft and flat, not bulging.
Incorrect. Adding more fluid without a prescription could worsen the problem.
Incorrect. Waiting 4 hours delays the response to an abnormal neurologic finding.
Correct. A normal fontanel is soft and flat; a bulging fontanel is abnormal and must be reported.
questions.rationale: In infants, the anterior fontanel is a window on fluid status. Normal is soft and flat; sunken suggests dehydration; bulging is also abnormal and needs to be reported. An infant who was sunken and dehydrated should become soft and flat with rehydration, so a bulging fontanel with new irritability is an unexpected change. The tempting error is to read "no longer sunken" as success, but overshooting to bulging is a red flag.
questions.takeaway: Fontanel: soft and flat is normal, sunken means dehydration, bulging is abnormal and must be reported.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three possible fontanel findings and what each means.
questions.hintStrategy: When a finding has moved past normal in the other direction, treat it as a new problem, not as improvement.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · Fluid & Electrolyte Assessment, Daily Weights & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with heart failure who gained 1.8 kg overnight and has new crackles
A client who lost 0.4 kg overnight after a planned dose of a diuretic
An 88-year-old with slow skin turgor, moist membranes, and a stable weight
A client with urine specific gravity of 1.028 who is drinking well
optionRationales: Correct. A rapid weight gain of 1.8 kg (about 1.8 L of fluid) with new crackles signals fluid retention affecting the lungs.
Incorrect. A small loss after a diuretic is the expected response.
Incorrect. Skin turgor is less reliable in older adults, and the moist membranes and stable weight do not suggest a deficit.
Incorrect. A specific gravity of 1.028 is within the normal range of 1.005–1.030.
questions.rationale: Daily weight is the most sensitive measure of fluid change, and 1 kg is about 1 L of fluid. A 1.8-kg overnight gain with new crackles suggests fluid overload that is already affecting breathing, which makes this client the priority. Slow skin turgor in an 88-year-old is tempting because it looks abnormal, but older adults' skin naturally loses elasticity, so the nurse relies more on weight, membranes, and I&O, which are reassuring here.
questions.takeaway: A rapid weight gain plus new crackles outranks expected or isolated findings.
questions.hintContent: Convert each weight change into fluid and check each value against its normal range.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out expected findings and normal values first; the client left with an unexpected breathing change goes first.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 70-kg client has an indwelling urinary catheter. The nurse reviews the hourly urine output (see exhibit). Vital signs are stable. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider that output is below the minimum
Check the catheter tubing for kinks or a blockage
Increase the IV fluid rate to improve kidney blood flow
Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline to clear it
optionRationales: Incorrect. The provider needs to know, but a quick check of the tubing may find a simple cause, and the report is more useful with that information.
Correct. With 2 consecutive hours below the minimum of 35 mL/hr, the nurse first rules out a mechanical cause, such as a kinked or blocked tube.
Incorrect. Changing the IV rate requires a prescription.
Incorrect. Catheter irrigation requires a prescription and is not the first step.
questions.rationale: Minimum urine output is 0.5 mL/kg/hr, which is 35 mL/hr for a 70-kg client. Output below that for 2 or more consecutive hours means the nurse reassesses, starting with making sure the catheter is not kinked or blocked and checking the bladder, and then notifies the provider. Assessing before acting prevents treating a "kidney problem" that is actually a bent tube. Notifying the provider is tempting because low output is serious, but checking the tubing takes seconds and changes what the nurse reports.
questions.takeaway: Low catheter output: check the tubing and bladder first, then notify the provider.
questions.hintContent: Calculate this client's minimum hourly output and consider simple causes of low drainage.
questions.hintStrategy: When an action and an assessment compete and the client is stable, assess first, especially a quick equipment check.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 4-year-old has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. The nurse finds dry, sticky mucous membranes, a urine specific gravity of 1.032, no tears when crying, and the child is now difficult to arouse. Which finding should the nurse report first?
options: Mucous membranes are dry and sticky
Urine specific gravity is 1.032
The child is difficult to arouse
The child has no tears when crying
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dry membranes confirm a fluid deficit but do not show organ effects.
Incorrect. A high specific gravity shows the kidneys are conserving water; it supports the deficit but is less urgent.
Correct. A change in level of consciousness shows the fluid and electrolyte problem is now affecting the brain, the most serious finding.
Incorrect. No tears is a sign of a deficit but is less serious than a change in neuro status.
questions.rationale: All four findings point to a fluid deficit, which helps confirm the problem, but priority depends on which one shows the greatest threat. Neuro status (level of consciousness, orientation, motor function) is part of every fluid and electrolyte assessment because the brain depends on normal fluid and electrolyte balance. A child who is now difficult to arouse has a decline in level of consciousness. The specific gravity is tempting because it is a hard number above the normal limit, but it reflects the kidneys conserving water, not organ failure.
questions.takeaway: When every finding fits a fluid deficit, a change in level of consciousness is reported first.
questions.hintContent: Ask which finding shows the deficit is now affecting a vital organ.
questions.hintStrategy: When all options are abnormal and point the same way, choose the one that shows the most serious consequence.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: During a morning assessment of an 86-year-old client, the nurse notes that a pinched skin fold on the forearm returns slowly. The mucous membranes are moist and pink, the weight is unchanged from yesterday, and 24-hour intake and output are balanced. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Notify the provider that the client needs IV fluids
Encourage the client to drink at least 3 L of fluid today
Start strict I&O and request a stat serum osmolality
Conclude that the overall data do not show a deficit
optionRationales: Incorrect. Requesting IV fluids based on one unreliable finding could cause fluid overload in an older adult.
Incorrect. A large fluid goal is not supported by the data and may be unsafe for an older adult.
Incorrect. Ordering tests for a single unreliable finding when other data are normal is not needed.
Correct. Older adults' skin naturally loses elasticity, so turgor is less reliable; moist membranes, stable weight, and balanced I&O do not support a fluid deficit.
questions.rationale: Skin turgor is tested by pinching a skin fold and watching how fast it returns. Older adults' skin naturally loses elasticity, so slow return is common even when hydration is normal, and the nurse relies more on weights, mucous membranes, and I&O. Here, every other indicator is reassuring. Calling for IV fluids is tempting because tenting usually means a deficit, but acting on an unreliable finding alone could cause harm.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, confirm slow skin turgor with weight, mucous membranes, and I&O before calling it a deficit.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aging affects the reliability of skin turgor.
questions.hintStrategy: When one finding conflicts with several others, ask whether that single finding is reliable in this client.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 67-year-old client is admitted with weakness after several days of poor fluid intake. The nurse reviews the admission results (see exhibit). Which result requires the nurse's follow-up?
options: Serum osmolality 312 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg
Urine specific gravity 1.024
Hematocrit 47% in this male client
optionRationales: Correct. Serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg means the blood is more concentrated than normal, consistent with a water deficit.
Incorrect. Urine osmolality of 640 is within the normal range of 200–800 mOsm/kg.
Incorrect. A specific gravity of 1.024 is within the normal 1.005–1.030 range.
Incorrect. A hematocrit of 47% is within the typical adult male range of about 42–52%.
questions.rationale: Normal serum osmolality is 280–300 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 200–800 mOsm/kg, specific gravity is 1.005–1.030, and the typical adult male hematocrit is about 42–52%. Only the serum osmolality is outside its range; at 312 it shows concentrated blood, and the body should respond with thirst and ADH release to conserve water. The urine osmolality is tempting because 640 sounds high, but healthy kidneys have a wide range for concentrating urine.
questions.takeaway: Serum osmolality above 300 means concentrated blood, a sign of water deficit.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal ranges for serum osmolality, urine osmolality, and specific gravity.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each value against its own range; a big number is not abnormal if its normal range is wide.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client received IV furosemide for fluid overload. This morning's weight is 3 kg lower than yesterday. As the client stands to walk to the bathroom, the client reports feeling dizzy, and the nurse notes a pale face. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the weight loss as a sign that the diuretic is working
Help the client sit or lie down and recheck the blood pressure and pulse
Encourage the client to drink two glasses of water right away
Notify the provider that the client lost 3 L of fluid overnight
optionRationales: Incorrect. The loss may reflect the diuretic's effect, but a dizzy, pale client needs immediate safety action, not documentation.
Correct. Dizziness on standing after a large fluid loss suggests the blood pressure is dropping with position; the first priority is preventing a fall, then measuring the vital signs.
Incorrect. Fluids may later be appropriate, but the client is at immediate risk of falling.
Incorrect. The provider needs to know, but the nurse first protects the client and gathers vital signs to report.
questions.rationale: A 3-kg overnight drop means about 3 L of fluid was lost. When blood volume drops, the heart rate rises and blood pressure may fall, especially when the client stands up, which explains the dizziness and pallor. Safety comes first: the nurse helps the client sit or lie down to prevent a fall, then rechecks blood pressure and pulse before notifying the provider. Calling the provider first is tempting because the loss is large, but leaving a dizzy client standing risks injury.
questions.takeaway: Dizziness on standing after rapid fluid loss: protect the client from falling first, then check vital signs.
questions.hintContent: Convert the weight change to fluid and think about what that volume loss does to blood pressure when standing.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client is at immediate risk of injury, choose the safety action before reporting or documenting.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews a 12-hour intake and output record for an 80-kg client (see exhibit). Which action should the nurse take?
options: Document the positive balance as expected with IV fluids
Encourage more oral fluids and recheck at the end of the next shift
Notify the provider that urine output is below minimum
Ask the assistive personnel to start a new I&O record
optionRationales: Incorrect. Some positive balance can occur with IV fluids, but urine below the minimum is not expected and must not be dismissed.
Incorrect. Waiting another shift delays reporting a finding that may mean poor kidney blood flow.
Correct. The minimum for an 80-kg client is 40 mL/hr, or 480 mL in 12 hours; 310 mL of urine is well below that and must be reported.
Incorrect. A new record does not address the low output that is already documented.
questions.rationale: Urine output should be at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr. For an 80-kg client that is 40 mL/hr, or 480 mL over 12 hours, so 310 mL is below the minimum even though the client took in more than 2 L. Low output with a large positive balance suggests the kidneys are not getting enough blood flow or are not working well, or that fluid is being retained, and the nurse reports it. Documenting it as an expected positive balance is tempting because the client is on IV fluids, but the urine number itself is the red flag.
questions.takeaway: Calculate the minimum (0.5 mL/kg/hr × hours) and report urine output below it, whatever the intake.
questions.hintContent: Multiply the weight by 0.5 and by the number of hours, then compare with the urine total.
questions.hintStrategy: In I&O exhibits, compare urine output with the client's calculated minimum before judging the balance.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with heart failure calls the home health nurse: "I weighed myself this morning after I urinated, same as always, and I'm 3 pounds heavier than yesterday. My ankles are a little puffy." What is the nurse's best response?
options: "Weigh yourself again tomorrow and call if it's still up."
"Drink less water tonight and see if the swelling goes down."
"A few pounds can change from day to day; that's normal."
"Please call your provider today about this weight gain."
optionRationales: Incorrect. Waiting another day lets fluid continue to build up.
Incorrect. The client should not self-treat without guidance; the gain needs evaluation.
Incorrect. A rapid gain over a day is almost always fluid, not normal variation.
Correct. A gain of 3 lb (about 1.4 kg, or roughly 1.5 L) in a day with new swelling suggests fluid retention that needs prompt provider follow-up.
questions.rationale: A rapid weight change over a day or two is almost always fluid, not fat or muscle. Three pounds is about 1.4 kg, which is roughly 1.5 L of retained fluid, and the client already has new ankle swelling. The client weighed correctly, so the number is trustworthy, and the nurse advises prompt contact with the provider. Telling the client to recheck tomorrow is tempting because it seems cautious, but it delays care while fluid continues to accumulate.
questions.takeaway: A rapid weight gain with new swelling is fluid until proven otherwise; report it the same day.
questions.hintContent: Convert pounds to kilograms to liters, and recall what a rapid daily change represents.
questions.hintStrategy: For home calls, choose the response that gets the client timely professional follow-up rather than watchful waiting.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who weighs 165 lb returns from surgery with an indwelling urinary catheter, and the nurse begins hourly urine output monitoring. What is the minimum hourly urine output the nurse should expect for this client?
options: 30 mL/hr
37.5 mL/hr
75 mL/hr
82.5 mL/hr
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is the minimum for a 60-kg client, not a 75-kg client.
Correct. 165 lb ÷ 2.2 = 75 kg; 75 kg × 0.5 mL/kg/hr = 37.5 mL/hr.
Incorrect. This uses 1 mL/kg/hr instead of 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Incorrect. This multiplies the weight in pounds by 0.5 without converting to kilograms.
questions.rationale: Minimum urine output is at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr. The weight must be in kilograms first: 165 lb ÷ 2.2 = 75 kg. Then 75 × 0.5 = 37.5 mL/hr, which is 300 mL over an 8-hour shift. The most common error is skipping the pound-to-kilogram conversion, which inflates the minimum and could make a normal output look low.
questions.takeaway: Minimum urine output = weight in kg × 0.5 mL/hr; convert pounds first.
questions.hintContent: Recall the urine output formula and the pound-to-kilogram conversion.
questions.hintStrategy: In calculation items, check units first; wrong answers are often built from a skipped conversion.

questions.ref: Module 6 · Fluids & Electrolytes · Fluid & Electrolyte Assessment, Daily Weights & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client receiving IV diuretics weighed 198.0 lb yesterday morning and 194.7 lb this morning on the same scale, after voiding, in the same gown. About how much fluid has the client lost?
optionRationales: Incorrect. This underestimates the loss; 3.3 lb is about 1.5 kg.
Correct. 3.3 lb × 0.45 kg/lb ≈ 1.5 kg, and 1 kg ≈ 1 L, so about 1.5 L of fluid was lost.
Incorrect. This treats each pound as 1 L; 1 lb is about 0.5 L.
Incorrect. This multiplies by 2.2 instead of dividing, which overestimates the loss.
questions.rationale: Because a rapid change over a day is almost always fluid, the nurse converts weight change to fluid volume. One kilogram equals about 1 liter, and 1 pound is about 0.45 kg, or roughly 0.5 L. A 3.3-lb drop is about 1.5 kg, or 1.5 L. Treating a pound as a liter is the most tempting error and doubles the estimate.
questions.hintContent: Convert the pound change to kilograms, then to liters.
questions.hintStrategy: Estimate before calculating: about half a liter per pound quickly rules out answers that are too large.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a stable client on intake and output monitoring. Which task is appropriate to assign to the assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Measure and record oral intake and urine output
Assess the client's mucous membranes and skin turgor
Interpret the 24-hour I&O balance and report concerns
Teach the client how to record intake at home
optionRationales: Correct. Measuring and recording I&O is a standard task within the AP's scope; the nurse interprets the totals.
Incorrect. Physical assessment is the nurse's responsibility.
Incorrect. Interpreting data and deciding what is a concern belongs to the nurse.
Incorrect. Teaching is a nursing responsibility.
questions.rationale: AP can measure and record intake and output, but the nurse interprets the totals and decides what they mean. Assessment, teaching, and interpretation are RN responsibilities. Interpreting the balance is tempting to delegate because the AP already has the numbers, but deciding whether a balance is concerning requires nursing judgment.
questions.takeaway: AP measure and record I&O; the nurse interprets it.
questions.hintContent: Separate collecting data from judging data.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation items, choose the task that is routine and measurable, with no assessment, teaching, or interpretation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 31-year-old client has been drinking large amounts of water. Results show urine specific gravity 1.003, urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg, and serum osmolality 276 mOsm/kg. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The body is short on water, and the kidneys are saving it
The body has excess water, and the kidneys are making dilute urine
The results show concentrated blood with concentrated urine
The kidneys are failing to respond to the client's fluid status
optionRationales: Incorrect. A water deficit would produce high serum osmolality and concentrated urine, the opposite of these results.
Correct. Serum osmolality below 280 shows dilute blood, and the low specific gravity and urine osmolality show the kidneys are appropriately excreting extra water.
Incorrect. Every value is on the low (dilute) side.
Incorrect. Dilute urine with dilute blood is the kidneys responding correctly.
questions.rationale: Serum osmolality (280–300 mOsm/kg) shows how concentrated the blood is, while urine osmolality (200–800 mOsm/kg) and specific gravity (1.005–1.030) show how concentrated the urine is. Here all three are low: the blood is diluted by extra water, and healthy kidneys respond by producing dilute urine to get rid of it. The option about kidney failure is tempting because the urine values are outside range, but low values in this setting show the kidneys doing their job.
questions.takeaway: Dilute blood plus dilute urine means the kidneys are correctly getting rid of extra water.
questions.hintContent: Decide whether each value is high or low, then ask what the kidneys should do in that situation.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the pattern across all the values rather than judging any one alone.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: During an 8-hour shift, a client ate 120 mL of gelatin, drank 240 mL of apple juice, and had 300 mL of ice chips. What intake should the nurse record?
options: 360 mL
510 mL
660 mL
810 mL
optionRationales: Incorrect. This leaves out the ice chips, which count as intake.
Correct. Gelatin 120 + juice 240 + ice chips counted at half volume (150) = 510 mL.
Incorrect. This counts the ice chips at full volume instead of half.
Incorrect. This counts the ice chips at full volume and then adds their half volume again.
questions.rationale: Intake includes all fluids and foods that are liquid at room temperature, such as gelatin, ice cream, and popsicles. Ice chips count as about half their volume in water because they are part air. So 120 + 240 + 150 = 510 mL. Counting ice chips at full volume is the most tempting error.
questions.takeaway: Count foods that are liquid at room temperature, and record ice chips at half their volume.
questions.hintContent: Recall which foods count as intake and how ice chips are converted.
questions.hintStrategy: List each item with its counted volume before adding, so no conversion is missed.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: An 11-month-old with dehydration from diarrhea has received IV rehydration for 12 hours. Which finding best indicates that the infant's fluid status is improving?
options: Urine specific gravity is 1.034
The infant has had one wet diaper in 8 hours
The anterior fontanel is soft and flat
The infant's eyes appear soft and sunken
optionRationales: Incorrect. A specific gravity above 1.030 means the kidneys are still conserving water.
Incorrect. Fewer wet diapers than usual suggests ongoing low output.
Correct. A soft, flat fontanel is the normal finding and shows fluid volume is being restored.
Incorrect. Soft, sunken eyes suggest a continuing fluid deficit.
questions.rationale: In an infant, signs of dehydration include a sunken fontanel, dry membranes, sunken eyes, fewer wet diapers, and concentrated urine. As rehydration works, these return toward normal: the fontanel becomes soft and flat, diapers are wet more often, and urine becomes less concentrated. The specific gravity is tempting because it is a lab number, but at 1.034 it still shows concentrated urine.
questions.takeaway: In infants, a soft, flat fontanel is a key sign that rehydration is working.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a normal fontanel feels like compared with a dehydrated one.
questions.hintStrategy: For "improving" items, choose the finding that has returned to normal, not one still showing the problem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 79-year-old client has been on bed rest in a supine position for 3 days, and the nurse suspects fluid retention. Where should the nurse check most carefully for pitting edema?
options: Over the sternum
On the forehead
On the back of the hand
Over the sacrum
optionRationales: Incorrect. The sternum is a site for checking skin turgor, not dependent edema.
Incorrect. The forehead is not a dependent area for a supine client.
Incorrect. The back of the hand is not dependent in a supine client and is not the key site.
Correct. In a client lying on the back, fluid collects in the lowest areas, so the sacrum is the key site to check.
questions.rationale: Edema is checked by pressing a finger into swollen tissue and seeing whether a dent remains. Extra tissue fluid collects in the lowest (dependent) parts of the body, which is often the feet and ankles in a client who is up and about and the sacrum in a client lying on the back. The sternum is tempting because it is a common skin assessment site, but it is used for turgor, a sign of fluid deficit.
questions.takeaway: Check for edema where gravity pulls fluid: the sacrum for a client on bed rest, the feet and ankles for one who is up.
questions.hintContent: Think about where gravity pulls fluid in a client who has been lying on the back.
questions.hintStrategy: Do not confuse sites for skin turgor (deficit) with sites for edema (excess).

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse taught a 68-year-old client with heart failure how to take daily weights at home. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I'll weigh myself whenever I remember during the day."
"I'll use the same scale every time I weigh myself."
"I'll weigh myself after I urinate and before breakfast."
"I'll wear about the same amount of clothing each day."
optionRationales: Correct. This statement needs correction; weights must be taken at the same time each day, usually early morning, to compare fluid changes.
Incorrect. Using the same scale is correct technique.
Incorrect. Weighing after voiding and before breakfast is correct technique.
Incorrect. Wearing the same amount of clothing is correct technique.
questions.rationale: Daily weights only reflect fluid change when everything else stays the same: same time (usually early morning after voiding and before breakfast), same scale, and same amount of clothing. Weighing at random times lets meals, drinks, and voiding change the number, so a real fluid gain could be hidden or a false one created. Each of the other statements describes correct technique, which makes them tempting to choose in a "needs teaching" item.
questions.takeaway: Daily weights: same time, same scale, same clothing, after voiding and before breakfast.
questions.hintContent: List the conditions that must stay the same for weights to be compared.
questions.hintStrategy: In "needs further teaching" items, look for the statement that is wrong; the correct statements are the distractors.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted after several days of vomiting and poor intake. Which findings support a fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.
options: Heart rate 112/min, up from a baseline of 76/min
Urine specific gravity 1.034
Dry, sticky oral mucous membranes
Hematocrit 51%
Crackles in both lung bases
Distended neck veins while sitting upright
optionRationales: Correct. When blood volume drops, the heart rate rises to keep blood moving.
Correct. A specific gravity above 1.030 shows concentrated urine as the kidneys save water.
Correct. Dry, sticky membranes suggest a fluid deficit.
Correct. A hematocrit above the typical female range (about 37–47%) suggests hemoconcentration from water loss.
Incorrect. Crackles suggest too much fluid, not a deficit.
Incorrect. Distended neck veins suggest fluid excess.
questions.rationale: A fluid deficit shows up in many systems at once: a faster heart rate as the body compensates, dry membranes, concentrated urine (specific gravity above 1.030), and a rising hematocrit as the same red cells are packed into less fluid. Because no single clue tells the whole story, the nurse looks for findings that point the same way. Crackles and distended neck veins are tempting to select in any fluid question, but they point to excess.
questions.takeaway: Fluid deficit: fast pulse, dry membranes, high specific gravity, and high hematocrit together.
questions.hintContent: Sort each finding into "too little fluid" or "too much fluid."
questions.hintStrategy: Decide the direction of the imbalance first, then select only findings that match it.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with heart failure is being assessed for fluid excess. Which findings support this concern? Select all that apply.
options: Weight up 1.6 kg since yesterday
New crackles in both lung bases
Distended neck veins with the head raised
2+ pitting edema of both ankles
Soft, sunken eyes
Urine specific gravity 1.034
optionRationales: Correct. A rapid gain of 1.6 kg is about 1.6 L of retained fluid.
Correct. Crackles can mean fluid in the lungs.
Correct. Swollen neck veins can go with too much fluid.
Correct. Pitting edema shows extra fluid in the tissues.
Incorrect. Sunken eyes suggest a fluid deficit.
Incorrect. Highly concentrated urine suggests the kidneys are saving water, as in a deficit.
questions.rationale: Fluid excess shows as rapid weight gain (1 kg ≈ 1 L), crackles in the lungs, distended neck veins, and edema in the tissues. The nurse puts these clues together and notifies the provider of a sudden gain with new edema or crackles. Highly concentrated urine is tempting to select because it is abnormal, but it signals the kidneys conserving water, which fits a deficit.
questions.takeaway: Fluid excess: rapid weight gain, crackles, distended neck veins, and edema.
questions.hintContent: Ask which findings show fluid accumulating in the vessels, lungs, or tissues.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, an abnormal finding is only correct if it matches the specific problem in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client after abdominal surgery has a nasogastric tube, a wound drain, and an indwelling catheter. Which items should the nurse include in the output total? Select all that apply.
options: Urine from the catheter bag
Nasogastric drainage
Wound drain output
Emesis
Fluid lost through sweating
Water vapor lost through breathing
optionRationales: Correct. Urine is the main measured output.
Correct. NG drainage is measured fluid leaving the body.
Correct. Drain output is measurable and counts.
Correct. Vomit is measured and recorded as output.
Incorrect. Sweat is an insensible loss; it cannot be measured, so it is not in the I&O total.
Incorrect. Water vapor from the lungs is an insensible loss and is not measured.
questions.rationale: Output includes all measurable fluid leaving the body: urine, liquid stool, emesis, nasogastric drainage, wound and drain output, and bleeding. These are sensible losses. Insensible losses, through the skin and lungs, cannot be measured and are not included in I&O totals, but they still affect hydration, especially with fever, heat, or fast breathing. Sweat is tempting to include because it is visible, but it cannot be accurately measured.
questions.takeaway: Output = every measurable loss (urine, stool, emesis, NG, drains, bleeding); insensible losses are not totaled.
questions.hintContent: Separate sensible (measurable) from insensible (unmeasurable) losses.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask: can this be collected and measured in milliliters?

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 62-year-old client is suspected of having a water deficit. The nurse wants data that show how concentrated the client's body fluids are. Which data should the nurse review? Select all that apply.
options: Serum osmolality
Urine specific gravity
Hematocrit
Urine osmolality
Serum potassium
Daily weight trend
optionRationales: Correct. Serum osmolality measures the concentration of particles in the blood.
Correct. Specific gravity shows how concentrated the urine is.
Correct. Hematocrit rises when blood is concentrated and falls when it is diluted.
Correct. Urine osmolality shows how much the kidneys are concentrating the urine.
Incorrect. Potassium is an electrolyte value, monitored separately with lab values.
Incorrect. Daily weight measures fluid volume, not concentration.
questions.rationale: The nurse monitors three things: volume (I&O, daily weights, physical assessment), concentration (serum and urine osmolality, specific gravity, hematocrit, and the type of IV fluid ordered), and electrolytes (lab values). When the body is short on water, the concentration measures tend to rise together. Daily weight is tempting because it is the best measure of fluid change, but it tracks volume, not concentration.
questions.takeaway: Concentration tools: serum and urine osmolality, specific gravity, and hematocrit.
questions.hintContent: Match each tool to volume, concentration, or electrolytes.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort options into categories first; select only the ones in the category the stem asks for.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old client is 2 days after surgery. The nurse compares today's vital signs with the preoperative baseline (see exhibit). Which current findings suggest the client's fluid volume is low or fluid losses are increasing? Select all that apply.
options: Heart rate 108/min
BP drops from 120/74 lying to 98/60 standing
Temperature 39.1°C
Respiratory rate 28/min and deep
Blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg sitting
Oxygen saturation 98% on room air
optionRationales: Correct. The heart rate rises to keep blood moving when volume drops.
Correct. A fall in blood pressure on standing suggests low circulating volume.
Correct. Fever increases fluid loss through the skin and lungs.
Correct. Fast, deep breathing increases insensible water loss through the lungs.
Incorrect. This is close to the client's baseline and does not suggest low volume.
Incorrect. A normal oxygen saturation does not reflect fluid volume.
questions.rationale: Vital signs are fluid clues, and each is compared with the client's own baseline. When volume drops, the heart rate rises and blood pressure may fall, especially on standing. Fever and fast, deep breathing increase insensible losses through the skin and lungs, which are not captured in I&O. A sitting blood pressure near baseline is tempting to select, but it does not suggest a deficit, which is why the nurse also checks the pressure on standing.
questions.takeaway: Rising pulse, a drop in BP on standing, fever, and fast breathing all point to low volume or increasing losses.
questions.hintContent: Compare each vital sign with the baseline and ask how it relates to volume or insensible loss.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the baseline given in the stem; a value is significant when it changes from the client's own normal.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the histories of several clients. None has bleeding or a recent blood transfusion. In which clients would the nurse expect the hematocrit to be higher than the client's usual level? Select all that apply.
options: Three days of vomiting with little oral intake
Working outdoors in the heat with heavy sweating
Several days of profuse watery diarrhea
Rapid infusion of 3 L of 0.9% sodium chloride
Drinking 6 L of plain water in a few hours
Several boluses of lactated Ringer's
optionRationales: Correct. Losing water concentrates the red cells in less plasma (hemoconcentration).
Correct. Heavy sweating removes water, so the hematocrit rises.
Correct. Fluid lost through diarrhea concentrates the blood.
Incorrect. Large volumes of isotonic fluid dilute the red cells, lowering the hematocrit.
Incorrect. Excess water dilutes the blood, lowering the hematocrit.
Incorrect. Isotonic boluses add plasma volume and dilute the hematocrit.
questions.rationale: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood made up of red cells, so it changes with the amount of fluid in the blood, not just the number of cells. When the body loses water through vomiting, sweating, or diarrhea, the same red cells are packed into less fluid and the hematocrit rises (hemoconcentration). When fluid is added, by isotonic IV fluids or large water intake, the hematocrit falls (hemodilution). The IV fluid options are tempting because they change volume, but they push the percentage down.
questions.takeaway: Water loss raises the hematocrit; added fluid lowers it.
questions.hintContent: Use the orange juice and pulp analogy: what happens to the percentage when water is removed?
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether each situation removes or adds water, then match the direction to the stem.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client's serum osmolality is 308 mOsm/kg after several days of low fluid intake. Which responses would the nurse expect the body to make? Select all that apply.
options: Increased thirst
Release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Kidneys conserving water
Urine with a higher specific gravity
Large volumes of pale, dilute urine
A drop in serum sodium concentration
optionRationales: Correct. When the blood is too concentrated, the body triggers thirst.
Correct. ADH is released so the kidneys hold on to water.
Correct. Under ADH's effect, the kidneys reabsorb water.
Correct. Conserving water produces concentrated urine with a higher specific gravity.
Incorrect. Dilute urine is how the body gets rid of extra water, the opposite situation.
Incorrect. Sodium is the main contributor to serum osmolality; with a water deficit it tends to rise, not fall.
questions.rationale: Serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg means the blood is too concentrated. The body responds by triggering thirst and releasing ADH so the kidneys hold on to water, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine with a higher specific gravity. Older adults have a decreased thirst sensation, so this client may not drink even when the signal is present. Pale, dilute urine is tempting because the kidneys are "responding," but that response belongs to excess water.
questions.takeaway: High serum osmolality: thirst plus ADH, so the kidneys save water and the urine concentrates.
questions.hintContent: Ask what the body does to correct blood that is too concentrated.
questions.hintStrategy: Predict the body's response first, then select the options that match your prediction.
